description: **Presence is now declared, never derived.** Every flag declares exactly one of `Required()`, `Optional()` or `Default(v)`, and every positional arg one of `ArgRequired()`, `ArgOptional()` or `ArgDefault(v)`. Declaring none or two is a registration-time hard error, `Default(nil)` is refused with a redirect to `Optional()`, and `ArgRequired(bool)` is gone. Optional flags deliver nil (bools become real tri-state), compound flags no longer get a silent empty default, a mutex member declares its own absence, a `Flag` struct literal no longer registers, the dumped schema carries `presence` on every flag and arg entry, MCP tool schemas take requiredness from the declaration (required bools now appear), help renders exactly one presence part per line, and `ctx.Provided(name)` reports whether the invocation caused a value.

**A custom validator runs on a supplied value only.** `ValidateFn` no longer runs against a declared `Default(v)` -- including a `RelativeToRoot` default, whose `infra` source is still the declaration deciding. It runs when the invocation caused the value (`cli`, `env`, `config`, `implied`), which is the same definition `CoRequired`, `Requires` and `ctx.Provided` use.

**Help output fixes.** A `RelativeToRoot` default now renders as its declaration (`[default: RelativeToRoot('MYAPP_ROOT', 'store')]`) instead of Go's internal struct form, and `--help`/`-h` after a command group's name shows the group's help whatever follows it (`myapp db --help ./path` no longer reports an unknown command).

**README explains the Go-shaped declaration surface.** The package README now states that the Go implementation is not a port of the Python or TypeScript ones: the surface is Go's own (functional options, typed constants, generics, a panic at registration), the presence options write an unexported field so a bypassing `Flag` struct literal fails to register instead of silently dropping its value, and what the three implementations hold identical is behavior rather than spelling.

**Choice flags: a choice is a declaration scope.** `ChoiceFlag(name, help, ...)` elects exactly one of its declared `Choice(name, help, flags...)` values, and each choice owns the flags that exist only while it is elected. `MemberChoiceFlag` with `MemberChoice(memberFlag, help, scope...)` is the member-spelled twin, where each choice is its own flag and no selector token is ever typed. The elected value reaches the handler as one `*Elected` carrying `Fields`, consumed by `GetElected` plus `Match`/`When` -- which are compile-checked references to the choice values themselves and exhaustive against the declaration at dispatch. Parsing stays order-independent, choice flags nest to any depth, and a flag supplied outside its elected scope is a distinct parse error naming the flag, its owning choice and the choice that was elected -- never "unknown flag".

**`MutexGroup` is removed.** Exactly-one-of-these is a member-spelled choice flag now, which carries the same rule with the type information kept rather than thrown away, gives each member a scope of its own, and reproduces the mutex error sentences byte-for-byte. There is no shim and no deprecation period: replace `WithMutex(MutexGroup{Flags: []Flag{...}})` with `WithFlags(MemberChoiceFlag(name, help, Required(), MemberChoice(...), ...))`. A member flag now declares `Required()` (read as *required once this member is elected*), inverting the old rule that forbade it, and the handler receives one tagged record instead of one value per member.

**A choices entry is always a record.** `Choices(...)` and `ArgChoices(...)` take `Ch(<value>, "<help>")` entries; the bare-value spelling is deleted, so `Choices("head", "tags")` becomes `Choices(Ch("head", "push only the current HEAD branch"), Ch("tags", ""))`. Help on an entry is optional -- `""` is the no-help spelling -- and a flag whose entries carry help renders as an indented block instead of the one-line `[choices: a, b]` form.

**`FlagOption` is an interface.** `type FlagOption interface{ applyFlag(*Flag) }` replaces the `func(*Flag)` type, which is what lets a choice be a value with identity that a handler switches on by reference. Every constructor keeps its signature -- `Required()` still returns `FlagOption` and still compiles at every call site. The one caller shape that breaks is a hand-written `strictcli.FlagOption` func literal, which could only ever reach `Flag`s exported fields, could not declare presence, and therefore already failed registration.

**A positional arg with helped choices renders an indented block.** The block rule was always content-keyed -- any `ArgChoices(Ch(value, help))` entry carrying help -- and it now reaches positional args exactly as it reaches flags: the entries render beneath the arg's line with their help, the one-line `[choices: a, b]` part is dropped in that form, and one alignment column is computed across the whole `Arguments:` section, deepest entry included.

**Choice-flag help lines are corrected.** A member-spelled selector renders its own name in the left column and `(exactly one of the following)` after its help text in the right one, with its member flags two columns beneath it rather than four; a payload-less member renders `--all-profiles` rather than `--all-profiles, --no-all-profiles`, because the negation declines rather than electing; and a defaulted selector renders the complete elected value, `[default: webhook (url=https://example.test/hook, retries=5)]`, instead of the choice name alone -- a choice whose scope is empty still renders `[default: <choice>]`, and a nested selector states its own default on its own line.

**A bare `ArgChoices` entry reports the arg, not a flag that does not exist.** `ArgChoices(strictcli.ChoiceValue{Value: "head"})` panicked with `Flag "target": choices entry 0 is a bare value`; it now reads `Arg "target": ...`, because both surfaces went through one validator that took the flag prefix as a constant.

**Sibling scopes reusing a short are now checked.** §24.7 lets two scopes that can never be live together claim one short, and two declarations that were silently accepted are refused at registration: `command "run": short '-t' is claimed by '--target' and '--tag' with different value shapes` when the reuse would make tokenization depend on the election, and `short '-t' is reused by sibling scopes and also claimed by '--transport', which elects` when one claimant is itself an election token. The claim table walks member scopes too, so two member flags sharing a short are refused by the second rule.

**A structural parse problem is now reported ahead of a value that will not parse.** An unknown flag, an unknown choice and a scope violation are facts about the command line's shape, and shape is decided before any token's text is interpreted -- on every command, not only on one that declares a choice flag. `myapp cmd --count abc --unknown` reported `--count: expected integer, got 'abc'` and now reports `unknown flag '--unknown'`, and the answer no longer depends on which token came first.

**`--dump-schema` writes schema version 2.** A flag or arg entry carries a real JSON Schema fragment under `value_schema`, from a closed subset of `type`, `items`, `additionalProperties` and `enum` with JSON Schema's own type names; the `type` key (`"list[str]"`, `"dict[str]"`) and the `repeatable` key are gone, because arity is a property of the value and a repeatable flag publishes the same array fragment a list-typed flag does. A value flag's `Choices(...)` splits in two: the values as an `enum` inside the fragment, and the value-plus-help records beside it under `choices` (`help` omitted when an entry declares none) -- and an integer choice beyond ±2^53 is refused at registration, because a reader that parses JSON numbers as IEEE-754 doubles reads a different integer back (declare a big identifier as a string; float choices are unaffected). A choice flag has no fragment at all -- its value is a variant the subset cannot express -- and instead publishes its nested choices and scopes, each scoped entry a full flag entry, with `elect_by` as the discriminator. Every entity's keys are emitted in a declared order rather than Go's map-marshal sort, and the document is written by a canonical writer (canonical floats, raw UTF-8, no HTML escaping, two-space indent, one trailing newline) so two implementations' dumps are byte-comparable. The `defaults` block is rewritten as the complete map of what an omitted key means, and the dump stops being blind to behavior: `config_format`, `config_path`, `config_conflict_mode`, per-flag `prefixed` and per-command `flag_sets` each appear exactly when a declaration departs from the framework's own behavior, `config_path` publishes the declaration rather than the machine's resolution of it, and the `checks` block is a function of the declaration alone rather than of whether a check has run in this process.

**The MCP tool schema describes array parameters correctly.** A parameter whose value is a list carried its `enum` at the property root, which said the array itself had to equal one of the choices; it now sits inside `items`, describing an element. The projection derives every parameter's shape from the same fragment the dumped `value_schema` publishes, so a tool schema and a dumped schema cannot disagree about a value's shape.

**A list-typed variadic arg may declare choices.** `NewArg("envs", help, ArgType(ListOf(TypeStr)), Variadic(), ArgChoices(...))` was refused with `choices is incompatible with list type` while the same arg declared with the scalar element type was accepted. The two spellings are one declaration with one published shape, so the ban is deleted and the entries are checked against the element type in both.

**The README documents the choice flag and the choices record.** The mutually-exclusive-flag-groups section is replaced by a choice-flag section covering `Choice`/`ChoiceFlag`, `MemberChoice`/`MemberChoiceFlag`, identity-checked `Match`/`When` over `*Elected`, and the presence rules; the choices section shows the `Ch(<value>, "<help>")` record spelling that replaced bare values; and the constructor list, flag-option table and core-type table follow.

**A payload-less member publishes no MCP property.** The electing member flag was projected as an ordinary scoped flag, so a member carrying no payload contributed a spurious boolean property beside the selector's own enum -- a second spelling of an election the enum already carries, and one no caller could usefully send. A payload-carrying member now contributes exactly its payload property, under its own name and with its own value schema, and a payload-less one contributes nothing at all.

**A member's payload key elects that member at the machine boundary.** The flat form `App.Call` and MCP take has no tokens, so supplying the property that flattens under a member's own flag name IS that election: `{"profile": "work"}` now elects `--profile` and carries its value, exactly as `--profile work` does on the command line. Supplying one member's payload beside a selector key naming a DIFFERENT member is a double election, and where it was previously accepted with the payload silently dropped it is now refused with the CLI's own sentence -- `--profile and --all-profiles are mutually exclusive` -- over MCP as an ordinary tool-result error.

**A member name colliding with a command-level flag is reported as the duplicate flag name it is, and an out-of-scope member flag names the scope that owns it.** Under member spelling a choice name IS a flag name: `MemberChoice(StringFlag("profile", ...), ...)` declared beside a command flag named `profile` now panics `command "run": duplicate flag name "profile"` instead of the unreachable-scoped-flag message. And a member flag supplied outside its scope reported `flag '--profile' is only valid under '--mode advanced --profile'`, appending the member's own election to the path it is missing from; it now stops at the scope that owns it, `'--mode advanced'`, while a flag declared INSIDE a member's scope keeps every segment.

**A choice name must match `[a-z][a-z0-9-]*`, checked at registration.** A choice name is a surface name whatever elects it: a token-spelled choice flag publishes it in an enum, and under member spelling it is the flag that elects the choice. `Choice("Email", ...)` and `MemberChoice(BoolFlag("all_profiles", ...), ...)` are now refused with `Flag "via": choice name "Email" must match [a-z][a-z0-9-]*`, in both spellings, where they registered before.

**A list carrier may declare choices.** `ListFlag(TypeStr, "tags", help, Unique(false), Choices(Ch("a", ...), Ch("b", ...)))` was refused at registration with `choices is incompatible with compound types (list/dict)` although the dumped `value_schema` and the MCP tool schema already published the enum inside `items`. Choices on a list carrier constrain each ELEMENT, and are checked per element on the command line, from an env var and on a declared default alike. The ban survives for a dict -- whose keys are structurally strings and whose values are not a closed set -- and now reads `Flag "header": dict type cannot be combined with choices`, the siblings' own sentence.
